definitions.def: to be extremely good at something
to practice something before doing it for real
real and genuine, not a copy
the act of controlling your own feelings or desires
something that encourages you to do something

grammar_choice.en_template: Our brains evolved this ability to create an internal mental picture or model of the world {{1:in which/which}} we can rehearse forthcoming actions, without the risks or the penalties of {{2:doing/to do}} them in the real world.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 우리 뇌는 실제 세계에서 행동할 때의 위험이나 대가 없이 다가올 행동을 미리 연습할 수 있는, 세계에 대한 내적 심상이나 모형을 만들어 내는 이 능력을 진화시켰다.
explain: 뒤 절이 완전 → 전치사+관계대명사 in which (= where).

explain: the same ~ as 동등 비교 → as.

jumble.answer: Our brains evolved this ability to create an internal mental picture or model of the world in which we can rehearse forthcoming actions, without the risks or the penalties of doing them in the real world.
There are even hints from brain-imaging studies by Harvard University psychologist Steve Kosslyn showing that your brain uses the same regions to imagine a scene as when you actually view one.
But evolution has seen to it that such internally generated representations are never as authentic as the real thing.
This is a wise bit of self-restraint on your genes' part.
If your internal model of the world were a perfect substitute, then anytime you felt hungry you could simply imagine yourself at a banquet, consuming a feast.
You would have no incentive to find real food and would soon starve to death.
As the Bard said, "You cannot cloy the hungry edge of appetite by bare imagination of a feast."
